# JetBrains' Next Move Isn't a Better IDE — It's a Governance Layer Over Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI

## The Real Story Here

JetBrains isn't trying to out-code Claude or Codex. They're positioning themselves as the control plane for teams that already use those tools. That's a fundamentally different bet than building a better autocomplete engine.

If this plays out, the IDE company becomes the policy enforcement point for AI-assisted development across your entire org. That matters more for security teams than another coding assistant ever could.

## What's Actually Happening

Engineering teams have spent the past few years picking up AI coding tools wherever they found them. Claude Code in one terminal. GitHub Copilot in VS Code. Gemini CLI for quick prototyping. Maybe Cursor for the developers who wanted something purpose-built.

The result: fragmentation. No single view of what's being generated, what's being accepted, and what's making it into production.

JetBrains appears to be building a governance layer that sits above these tools rather than replacing them. The approach acknowledges what's already true on the ground — developers aren't waiting for permission to use AI assistants, and they're not consolidating on a single vendor anytime soon.

According to reporting from The New Stack, JetBrains is developing capabilities that let teams manage AI tool usage across their organization. The focus isn't on generating better code. It's on visibility and control: who's using what, what policies apply, and how do you enforce them consistently.

This is a different posture than we've seen from most IDE vendors. Instead of "use our AI, it's better," the message is closer to "use whatever AI you want, we'll help you govern it."

[UNVERIFIED] The specific products or features JetBrains plans to ship aren't fully detailed in available sources. Whether this becomes a standalone product, an extension to existing IDEs, or something else entirely remains unclear.

## Why Practitioners Should Care

### The Visibility Problem Is Real

Most security teams I've talked to have no idea what AI tools developers are actually using. Shadow IT was annoying when it was a rogue SaaS subscription. Shadow AI is a different category of risk.

When a developer pastes proprietary code into Claude, accepts a suggestion, and commits it — what's the audit trail? For most orgs right now, there isn't one. The code just appears in the repo like any other commit.

A governance layer that actually sees these interactions changes the game for AppSec. You could answer questions like:

- Which AI tools are developers using, and how often?
- What percentage of committed code originated from AI suggestions?
- Are developers pasting sensitive data into external AI services?
- Which teams are following your AI usage policies, and which aren't?

Without visibility, you're guessing. And "we'll figure it out eventually" isn't a security posture.

### Policy Enforcement at the Right Layer

The interesting architectural choice here is where governance happens. You could try to enforce policies at the network layer (block certain domains), at the repo layer (scan commits after the fact), or at the identity layer (restrict who can access what).

JetBrains is betting that the IDE layer — or more precisely, the development environment layer — is where enforcement actually works. That's where you can intercept the interaction before code gets generated, before sensitive context gets sent to an external API.

If you're thinking about data loss prevention for AI tools, this matters. Network-level blocking is crude. Commit-time scanning is too late. Policy enforcement at the point of interaction is the only place you can actually prevent problems rather than detect them after the fact.

### The Multi-Tool Reality

Here's what I think JetBrains is actually responding to: developers aren't loyal to one AI assistant.

Different tools work better for different tasks. Claude might be the best for explaining legacy code. Copilot might generate boilerplate faster. Gemini CLI might integrate better with Google Cloud workflows. Cursor might feel better for certain languages.

Telling developers "pick one" hasn't worked. Pretending your org only uses one tool hasn't worked either.

A governance layer that's agent-agnostic — that can apply consistent policies across Claude, Codex, Gemini, and whatever ships next quarter — solves a real organizational problem. You stop having separate conversations about each tool and start having one conversation about AI-assisted development.

## The Competitive Landscape

JetBrains isn't the only company thinking about this problem.

GitHub is building governance features into Copilot Enterprise. That makes sense for orgs already standardized on GitHub's toolchain, but it only covers Copilot. If your developers are also using Claude Code or Cursor, you're back to fragmentation.

Microsoft's broader AI governance story spans Azure, M365, and Copilot — but it's enterprise-wide governance, not developer-specific. The abstractions are too high for security teams that need to understand code-level interactions.

Smaller players like Codeium and Tabnine have enterprise features, but they're trying to be the AI tool you use, not the governance layer over tools you already have.

JetBrains' positioning is different: we're not the AI, we're the control plane for AI. That's either a smart strategic move or a concession that they can't compete with Anthropic and OpenAI on model quality. Probably both.

[UNVERIFIED] I haven't seen detailed competitive analysis on how JetBrains' governance features compare feature-by-feature with GitHub Copilot Enterprise's admin controls.

## What This Means for Different Roles

### For Security Teams

If this works, you might finally have a single pane of glass for AI tool governance. One place to define policies, one place to check compliance, one place to investigate incidents.

The questions you'd want answered:

- Can you enforce context filtering? (Preventing sensitive code or secrets from being sent to AI services)
- Can you require approval workflows for AI usage on certain repos or projects?
- Can you integrate with your existing SIEM/SOAR for AI-related events?
- Can you prove compliance with SOC 2 / ISO 27001 controls around AI usage?

### For Engineering Leads

You're probably already dealing with inconsistent AI adoption across your teams. Some people swear by Claude, others haven't touched it. Some teams have informal guidelines, others have none.

A governance layer gives you standardization without prohibition. You can say "use what works for you, within these boundaries" and actually mean it.

### For Developers

The cynical view: another layer of surveillance from management.

The practical view: if the alternative is IT blocking AI tools entirely, a governance layer with reasonable policies is the better outcome. Most developers would rather have monitored access than no access.

The concern is always overhead. If governance means friction on every AI interaction, adoption will suffer. If it's invisible until you violate a policy, it's probably fine.

## [CHRIS TAKE]

## What to Watch

### JetBrains' Execution Timeline

Announcements are easy. Shipping is hard. The question is whether JetBrains can deliver something usable before the market consolidates around a different approach.

GitHub has momentum. Microsoft has distribution. JetBrains has developer trust in certain ecosystems (especially JVM languages), but that trust doesn't automatically transfer to a new product category.

### Integration Depth

A governance layer is only useful if it actually integrates with the tools developers use. That means:

- Official plugins or extensions for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI
- API-level integration that captures context and prompts, not just outputs
- Support for tools that might not want to be governed

That last point is tricky. Will Anthropic and OpenAI cooperate with third-party governance tooling? Will they view it as a competitive threat? The answer isn't obvious.

### Enterprise Adoption Signals

Watch for announcements from large enterprises adopting this approach. If Fortune 500 security teams start mandating JetBrains governance tooling, that's a strong signal. If adoption stays limited to existing JetBrains shops, the strategy isn't working.

## What to Do Next

**If you're evaluating AI governance today:**

Don't wait for JetBrains to ship. You need policies now, even if enforcement is manual. Document what AI tools are approved, what data can be shared, and what the review process is for AI-generated code. You can automate enforcement later.

**If you're a JetBrains shop:**

Keep an eye on this. If you're already using IntelliJ or other JetBrains IDEs, adopting their governance tooling might be the path of least resistance. But don't commit until you see what they actually ship.

**If you're evaluating Copilot Enterprise:**

Compare governance features carefully. GitHub's built-in governance is easier to adopt if you're all-in on their ecosystem. JetBrains' approach might be better if your developers use diverse tools.

**If you're not thinking about AI governance yet:**

Start. The longer you wait, the harder this gets. Developers are already using AI tools, and that usage is already creating risks you're not measuring.

## The Open Question

Here's what I keep coming back to: is there actually a market for tool-agnostic AI governance, or will enterprises just standardize on one vendor's stack and use that vendor's built-in controls?

JetBrains is betting on fragmentation. They're betting that developers will keep using multiple AI tools, and that enterprises will pay for a layer that governs them all. That's not unreasonable — it matches what I see on the ground today.

But consolidation is also possible. If one AI coding assistant gets good enough, developers might stop switching between tools. If GitHub's Copilot captures enough market share, organizations might just standardize and use GitHub's governance features.

What's your org doing? Are you trying to govern multiple AI tools, or are you standardizing on one? And if you're standardizing, how's that actually working with developers who have different preferences?
